assignments.title: The Drowsy Patient
assignments.description: The morning report is ready. Three patients are waiting.

assignments.title: Which Patient First?
assignments.description: Four rooms, a changing morning and a team to work with.

assignments.title: Afternoon Handoff
assignments.description: The afternoon handoff is yours. Take a look, then decide your next step.

mapping: A1 / priority
answers.priority: 12,14,9,charts
Not mapped
Its rationale already teaches the alertness cue. Retain the original choice but do not infer later independent cue recognition.
A1 / cues

C1; Accepted if both essentials selected, otherwise Revisit
All actual cue submissions follow priority feedback. Conservatively assisted, including after a correct priority response.
A1 / action

C2 + C3; escalate Accepted; stop Unsafe; other actions Revisit
Cue rationale precedes every action in the source sequence. All actual choices are assisted, regardless of label.

C3; a Accepted, b/c Revisit
Cue teaching and a scripted response-team path precede SBAR. Assisted. ABG/priority remain in snapshots but are not mapped or default-labelled Accepted.

Not a mapped component
An unacceptable dispatch creates a safer-path bridge; downstream mapped evidence is assisted. The original dispatch stays separate from the story plan.

C1 + C2 proxy: A/B/C Accepted; D Revisit; E Unsafe; F Outside role + Unsafe. V5 iii Unsafe.

Uses the existing primaryReason severity order. D3 heading already instructs coverage and response. Accepted choices support arranged response within a prompt, not independent discovery of a vital trend.

Independent only without prior D2/D3 bridges or a hint/retry. D4 explicitly prompts a call. Scope is the chosen contact/timing within that prompt.
A2 / report

C3: trend required; dressing additionally required only if revealed. Missing required item Revisit.

Never requires an unseen finding. Prior D2/D3/help bridge excludes independent evidence. Generated report contains selected observations plus the existing fixed concern/request scaffold; it does not measure free SBAR composition.
A3 / action
call: reassess,information,notify,escalate; specific information ID
C3: escalate Accepted; reassess Unsafe; information/notify Revisit
Committed and saved before the concern/findings options appear. Chart inspection is optional, not a hint. No independent claim is made for retries.
A3 / findings
findings: select two or three from confusion,hr,rr,bp,temperature,saturation,pillow,menu
C1: at least two of confusion,hr,rr,bp,temperature Accepted; otherwise Revisit

Oxygen saturation changes numerically (96→94) but is excluded from the draft qualifying set, following the supplied rule. The unfinished menu is also not a qualifying core cue. Review both restrictions for fairness.
A3 / concern
concern: infection,dehydration,medication,glucose,acute,tired,none
C2: acute hypothesis must satisfy the linked-finding rules below; tired/none Revisit
No single diagnosis is required. A tentative medication or glucose concern is not confirmation; missing exposure/glucose information is disclosed in teaching.

handoff.intro: Helen Ortiz, 81, day 2 for a urinary tract infection and dehydration, on IV antibiotics. Aide’s note at 1330: “A little confused, probably sundowning, she’s tired.” She’s yours for the afternoon.
handoff.history: Lives alone, independent. Her daughter said on admission: “Sharp as a tack.”
handoff.note: 0800 nursing note: Alert and oriented, chatting about her grandkids. Filled out her menu.
handoff.bedside: Unsure where she is, picking at the sheets. The menu slip is half-finished. She asks for a different pillow.

calls.title: Continue and reassess
calls.detail: Continue the current plan with bedside follow-up.

calls.title: Get specific information
calls.detail: Choose the assessment or information you would obtain now.

calls.title: Notify the provider
calls.detail: Inform the provider through the non-urgent process for review and decisions.

calls.title: Escalate now
calls.detail: Request urgent bedside evaluation through the provider or rapid response, following the hospital process.

information: Full bedside assessment, repeat vitals and level of consciousness
Clarify usual orientation and compare with the chart
Inspect the wound and obtain a full set of vitals
concerns: An acute cause, not sure which yet

checks.title: Bedside glucose
checks.result: Glucose 108 mg/dL in this fictional example. This does not explain the confusion as current hypoglycaemia; it does not rule out other acute causes.

checks.title: Full vitals and level of consciousness
checks.result: Repeat vitals match the 1400 flowsheet. She remains disoriented. Reassessment confirms the reported pattern; bedside evaluation should not be delayed.

checks.title: IV site and other possible sources
checks.result: IV site clean, no redness or swelling. This local finding does not rule out infection elsewhere or establish its source.

checks.title: Pain or urination
checks.result: No new pain reported; urine is more concentrated than this morning. This may add context but does not establish a cause or explain away the other findings.

concernRules: Any two or more qualifying changed findings.
At least two qualifying changes AND temperature selected; OR new confusion plus HR, RR or BP.
New confusion AND HR, RR or BP selected. Tentative acute hypothesis only; not a demonstrated cause.
Revisit for this complete A3 case.

exampleConcerns.label: An acute cause, not sure which yet

rewinds.title: Another oxygen reading
rewinds.history: 71-year-old with COPD and pneumonia, newly sleepy since 0400. No earlier chronic drowsiness. A pending blood gas has not resulted.
facts: Still opens his eyes to his name, then drifts off mid-sentence.
RR 10, shallow. SpO₂ now 99% on the existing prescribed oxygen.
HR 108, BP 152/90, temperature 38.2°C. No other improvement reported.
rewinds.rationale: A higher saturation does not explain persistent reduced alertness and slow, shallow breathing. Urgent bedside help is supported without waiting for a blood gas.
rewinds.alternatives: Assessment continues while help comes. Non-urgent notification or information gathering alone would delay the response to the current findings.

rewinds.title: After lunch
rewinds.history: Complete alternative history: admitted with improving pneumonia, no new drowsiness overnight and no sedating medicine in this branch. Daughter reports a usual after-lunch nap.
facts: Sleepy after lunch but wakes easily to voice, answers clearly and remains engaged.
RR 18 with normal effort; no new breathing difficulty. SpO₂ 97% on unchanged prescribed oxygen.
HR 88, BP 128/76, temperature 37.0°C, unchanged from the morning assessment.
rewinds.rationale: The reported explanation fits the current alertness, breathing and unchanged observations. Continue bedside follow-up rather than assuming an acute deterioration.
rewinds.alternatives: Clarifying the usual pattern or repeating the assessment is reasonable. Escalation is not required by the stated findings; escalate if new concern appears.

rewinds.title: A different bedside check
rewinds.history: 71-year-old with COPD and pneumonia. Earlier this morning he was alert, RR 18; saturation 97% on the current prescribed oxygen.
facts: Now wakes to voice but drifts off mid-sentence. RR 12; oxygen reading remains 97%.
HR 96, BP 132/78, temperature 37.2°C. No increased work of breathing reported.
A full bedside assessment and repeat observations have not yet been obtained.
rewinds.rationale: A full assessment and recheck now clarify the new reduction in alertness. The saturation does not explain it. Reassessment must be immediate, not a plan to wait.
rewinds.alternatives: Provider notification or urgent bedside escalation is also reasonable for the new change or local criteria. This is a borderline draft and needs explicit reviewer agreement.

rewinds.title: Inside the outline
rewinds.history: Room 414, arriving at 0733 after surgery ended at 0300. At 0700 HR 88 and BP 128/74. No new dressing spread has been observed in this branch.
facts: HR 112, BP 98/60, RR 20. Pale, lightheaded and anxious.
Drainage remains inside the 0600 outline.
The repeated bedside observations confirm the trend reported at 0730.
rewinds.rationale: The rising heart rate, falling BP and symptoms support urgent evaluation even without dressing expansion. The trend is enough to call; do not infer a bleeding diagnosis from the outline alone.
rewinds.alternatives: Continue assessment while requesting help. Information gathering alone or non-urgent notification does not match this confirmed symptomatic deterioration.

rewinds.title: A call from the family
rewinds.history: Complete alternative recovery: at 0700 HR 90, BP 126/74, comfortable. There was no earlier report of a falling BP or lightheadedness.
facts: At 0733 HR 90, BP 126/74, RR 16, SpO₂ 97%, temperature 36.9°C; comfortable and alert.
Dressing unchanged and drainage inside its outline. No new symptoms.
His daughter calls the desk for an update.
rewinds.rationale: A family request does not change the patient’s current condition. Continue routine assessment and provide an update through the appropriate process.
rewinds.alternatives: Escalation for acute deterioration is not supported by these unchanged observations. Concerns not stated here would require a new assessment.
rewinds.focus: Match the response to the findings

rewinds.title: At the dressing
rewinds.history: Complete alternative recovery: at 0700 HR 90 and BP 126/74; comfortable, no prior hypotensive trend. Drainage was at the marked edge.
facts: At 0733 HR 90, BP 126/74, RR 16, SpO₂ 97%, temperature 36.9°C; alert and comfortable.
A small area of drainage is just past the outline; amount and wound appearance have not yet been assessed.
No dizziness, faintness or other deterioration reported.
rewinds.rationale: Inspect the wound and obtain full observations now to clarify the small new finding. The stable bedside picture does not itself require urgent help.
rewinds.alternatives: Non-urgent provider notification is reasonable. Reassess the urgency if the inspection or trend is concerning. Exact appearance/amount remains an unresolved draft detail.

rewinds.title: Temperature check
rewinds.history: Helen Ortiz, 81, day 2 for UTI and dehydration on IV antibiotics. Independent at baseline; no known chronic confusion. At 0800 alert, HR 84, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO₂ 96%, temperature 37.2°C.
facts: At 1400 newly unsure where she is and picking at the sheets.
HR 106, BP 106/62, RR 24, SpO₂ 94%; temperature 37.0°C.
The aide’s “probably sundowning” explanation has not been established as her usual pattern.
rewinds.rationale: The absence of fever does not rule out sepsis. Assess the whole clinical picture, including changes from baseline. These combined changes support urgent bedside evaluation; the cause is not established.
rewinds.alternatives: Assessment and the hospital’s sepsis or deterioration process can proceed together. Non-urgent notification alone understates the current concern.
rewinds.focus: Look at the whole current picture

rewinds.title: A fuller admission history
rewinds.history: History updated throughout: Helen has had memory problems for months and usually becomes confused in the afternoons. Her daughter described that pattern on admission; there is no “sharp as a tack” history or new decline in this branch. The 0800 note described her usual morning orientation.
facts: At 1400 her orientation matches the daughter’s usual afternoon description; she engages and reports no new symptoms.
HR 84, BP 132/78, RR 16, temperature 37.2°C, SpO₂ 96%, matching 0800.
No new difficulty breathing, perfusion change or distress is reported.
rewinds.rationale: This description fits a documented baseline pattern with unchanged observations. Continue assessment without treating chronic cognitive difficulty as proof of a new acute cause.
rewinds.alternatives: Compare with usual orientation or inform the provider if uncertainty remains. A known pattern does not prevent acute illness; escalate for a new change or concern.

rewinds.title: After physical therapy
rewinds.history: Helen remains independent at cognitive baseline. At 0800 alert and oriented; she has just completed physical therapy at 1400. No earlier afternoon confusion is present in this branch.
facts: Oriented and answering clearly; says she is tired after physical therapy.
HR 84, BP 132/78, RR 16, temperature 37.2°C, SpO₂ 96%, matching 0800.
No new confusion, breathing difficulty or other symptom is reported.
rewinds.rationale: Tiredness after activity fits the stated current findings. Continue follow-up; escalation for a worsening pattern is not supported when that pattern is absent.
rewinds.alternatives: New symptoms or uncertainty would justify reassessment and a different response. No conclusion about infection resolution is established.
rewinds.focus: Keep the plan when the picture fits

sources.title: FDA: Pulse Oximeters
sources.scope: Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation and should be interpreted with symptoms. It does not validate a reassuring saturation as a reason to dismiss a change in breathing or alertness.

sources.title: OpenStax: Clinical Judgment Measurement Model overview
sources.scope: Educational framework for recognising and analysing cues and taking action. This mapping is an authored interpretation, not an endorsed or validated assessment.

sources.title: CDC: About Sepsis
sources.scope: General symptom constellation and need for evaluation. Does not diagnose the fictional patient or validate the response rules.

sources.title: CDC: Caring for Patients with Sepsis
sources.scope: Prompt evaluation and use of the facility’s policies and procedures. No treatment orders or national bedside response threshold are inferred.

sources.title: NICE NG253: Could this be sepsis?
sources.scope: Changes from usual behaviour and circulation or respiration, including presentations without high temperature. UK guidance supports teaching principles; it is not a US hospital protocol.

sources.title: OpenStax: Hypovolemic Shock
sources.scope: Concern about a postoperative vital-sign trend; no diagnosis of bleeding is established by the limited initial observations.

sources.title: AHRQ PSNet: Rapid Response Systems
sources.scope: Escalation principles, with local criteria and process. No medication, oxygen or device changes are instructed.

unresolved: A1: priority feedback identifies the alertness cue before cue selection, and cue teaching precedes action/SBAR. All mapped choices in the unmodified sequence are conservatively assisted. No independent card or Strong claim is produced. Review whether a later teaching-flow revision is warranted.
A2: D3 is a coverage/action proxy, not a separate cue-recognition or false-reassurance test. D4 explicitly prompts a call. Confirm the limited feedback wording and mapping.
A1 middle branch: new drifting off can justify urgent escalation despite otherwise stable observations. Confirm assessment-now, notification and escalation alternatives.
A2 middle branch: specify clinically meaningful amount/appearance and local wound reporting expectations before learner release.
A3: confirm urgency and hospital-process wording, plausible combined change, and fairness as an application case.
A3: medication effect or hypoglycaemia remains an unconfirmed acute hypothesis; accept only with acute findings and matched escalation, with no diagnosis claim.

A3 Rewind has two reassessment branches and no artificially constructed middle-urgency branch, following the updated build request’s clinical-coherence priority. Confirm this departure from the draft balance table.
Confirm that the three cases test the same component sufficiently for a formative comparison. No causal learning-effect claim is made.

scenario.title: The Drowsy Patient
scenario.reviewStatus: Independent nurse approval reported by the founder
scenario.report: Good morning. Report just ended. You have 3 patients on a med-surg unit.

patients.label: COPD / pneumonia
patients.report: 71-year-old with COPD, admitted 2 days ago for pneumonia. On oxygen by nasal cannula; the flow was turned up overnight because "his sats were dipping." "He's been really sleepy since about 0400, but his sats are great, 97%. Probably just tired, he didn't sleep well."
patients.feedback: A new change in level of consciousness is never "just tired" until you prove it. "Great sats" in a patient with COPD whose oxygen was just turned up is a cue, not reassurance.

patients.label: Post-op day 1
patients.report: 45-year-old, post-op day 1 after laparoscopic abdominal surgery. Pain 7/10, asking for pain medication. Vitals stable at 0600.
patients.feedback: Pain matters. Let Room 14 know you'll be back soon, or ask a colleague to check in. But pain with stable vitals is expected post-op; new drowsiness is not.

patients.label: Discharge teaching
patients.report: 58-year-old admitted for cellulitis, going home this morning. Needs discharge teaching. Stable overnight.
patients.feedback: Stable and expected. Discharge teaching can wait until your sicker patients are safe.

charts.text: Review all three charts at the station first
charts.feedback: Report already flagged a change in consciousness. See the patient.

scenario.bedside: You're at Room 12's bedside. Tap each finding to see it.
scenario.cuePrompt: Which findings worry you most right now? Select all that apply.

cues.label: Consciousness
cues.text: Opens his eyes to his name, then drifts off mid-sentence

cues.label: Heart rate
cues.text: Heart rate 108, sinus tachycardia on the monitor

cues.label: Medication record
cues.text: MAR: an as-needed sedating cough medication was given at 0300

scenario.essentialFeedback: Declining consciousness plus inadequate breathing is the problem that matters most.
scenario.supportingFeedback: They support the picture of inadequate ventilation, and sedation, infection and fever can all make breathing worse.
scenario.glucoseFeedback: A gentle note: it doesn't explain the drowsiness.
scenario.teaching: SpO2 estimates arterial oxygen saturation. It does not measure how effectively a patient eliminates CO2. CO2 retention is a strong concern here, but not yet a confirmed cause.

actions.text: Stay with him. Check his airway and breathing: rouse him, sit him upright, count his respirations, watch his effort. Call for help: activate rapid response per your facility's criteria and notify the provider.
actions.feedback: A new change in mental status with slow, shallow breathing meets typical rapid response criteria. Any staff member can call; you don't need permission. Act on the patient; labs come second.

actions.text: Wait for the ABG drawn at 0645 to result, then decide
actions.feedback: The patient in front of you is the emergency. A pending lab should never delay escalation.

actions.text: Turn the oxygen up because he's drowsy
actions.feedback: More oxygen can worsen CO2 retention in this patient. Oxygen changes follow orders or protocol.

actions.text: Turn the oxygen off because it's causing the problem
actions.feedback: Stopping oxygen suddenly can drop oxygen levels dangerously. Changes follow orders or protocol.

actions.text: Let him sleep and recheck in an hour, his oxygen is fine
actions.feedback: This is the trap the scenario teaches. His oxygen is fine; his breathing is not.

actions.text: Medicate Room 14 first, then come back
actions.feedback: Room 14 is stable. Room 12 is getting worse now.

scenario.abgArrival: The rapid response team arrives within minutes and starts evaluating him. While they work, the ABG drawn at 0645 under an existing order results.

interpretations.text: Respiratory acidosis with an elevated bicarbonate
interpretations.feedback: pH 7.26 shows acidemia; PaCO2 68 identifies a respiratory acidifying process. HCO3 30 is elevated. Compensation can raise bicarbonate, but this result alone does not establish chronic CO2 retention or exclude a mixed disorder.
The respiratory process is right, but HCO3 is elevated, not unchanged. Acute buffering can already raise bicarbonate; its value alone does not tell us the duration or adequacy of compensation.

The pH is still acidemic at 7.26. Compensation moves pH toward normal; it does not necessarily restore a normal pH. A normal-range pH would not, by itself, establish appropriate compensation or exclude a mixed disorder.

A pH below 7.35 is acidemia, not the name of the underlying process. The high PaCO2 supports respiratory acidosis. Elevated HCO3 does not make metabolic alkalosis the primary explanation; a concurrent metabolic process still needs context.
PaO2 88 on supplemental oxygen does not make this ABG normal. Acidemia and elevated PaCO2 remain important, and PaO2 does not measure ventilation.

scenario.deeper: In a simple respiratory acidosis, HCO3 typically rises about 1 to 2 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2 acutely, and about 3 to 4 with chronic renal compensation, relative to a usual baseline near PaCO2 40 and HCO3 24. These are approximate checks, not diagnoses. HCO3 30 does not prove chronic retention or acute-on-chronic disease. Prior blood gases, chemistry, timing and other clinical findings are needed; a mixed disorder remains possible.
scenario.sbarPrompt: The provider calls back while the team is at the bedside. Which SBAR is strongest?

parts: I'm the nurse for Room 12, a 71-year-old with COPD and pneumonia. He's become hard to keep awake since about 0400, and I've activated a rapid response.
His oxygen was turned up overnight, and he got an as-needed sedating cough medication at 0300.
RR 10 and shallow, SpO2 97% on oxygen, HR 108, BP 152/90, temp 38.2. New headache, flushed skin. ABG at 0645: pH 7.26, PaCO2 68, HCO3 30, PaO2 88. I'm concerned his ventilation is inadequate.
I need you at the bedside now. Please evaluate him and give orders for his oxygen and breathing support.
sbars.feedback: Clear concern, the data behind it, a specific request with a time frame.

sbars.text: "Hi, Room 12 is pretty sleepy and his ABG is off, but his sats are fine. Can you look at him when you get a chance?"
sbars.feedback: "Sats are fine" downplays the problem, and "when you get a chance" sets no urgency.

sbars.text: A full list of every vital sign and lab since admission, with no stated concern or request.
sbars.feedback: The provider has to guess what you're worried about.

outcome: With the provider now at the bedside, the team moves Room 12 to a higher level of care for breathing support.
takeaways: SpO2 estimates arterial oxygen saturation. It does not measure how effectively a patient eliminates CO2. When a patient gets sleepy, check their breathing, not just their sats.
When breathing and consciousness change, act on the patient. Labs confirm; they don't decide whether you call for help.
why: In some patients with COPD, too much supplemental oxygen can raise CO2. The main reasons: oxygen relaxes blood vessels in poorly ventilated parts of the lung, which worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and oxygen-rich blood holds less CO2 (the Haldane effect). The old "hypoxic drive" explanation plays only a small role.
Other things can slow breathing too: sedating medications, tired breathing muscles, and worsening pneumonia. In a real patient, several may be happening at once.
That's why many providers order a target SpO2 of 88 to 92% for patients at risk of CO2 retention, then adjust it based on blood gases and the individual patient.
scenario.remember: drowsiness or confusion, slow or shallow breathing, headache, warm flushed skin, and a "great" SpO2 on more oxygen than usual.
scenario.ask: Why can SpO2 look normal when CO2 is high?
scenario.share: I caught the hidden breathing problem in Room 12. Can you? theclinicaledge.org

references.title: BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings (O'Driscoll et al., Thorax, May 2017), hospital summary
references.scope: 88 to 92% target for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (Screens 4 and debrief)

references.title: Abdo WF, Heunks LMA. Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD: myths and facts. Critical Care 16, 323 (2012)
references.scope: V/Q mismatch as the main mechanism, Haldane effect as secondary, hypoxic drive as minor (debrief)

references.title: Merck Manual Professional: Primary Changes and Compensations in Simple Acid-Base Disorders
references.scope: Approximate acute/chronic bicarbonate responses in simple disorders; does not establish this patient's baseline (Screen 5)

references.title: Merck Manual Professional: Acid-Base Disorders
references.scope: Acidemia versus acidosis, expected compensation and mixed disorders (Screen 5)

references.title: AHRQ PSNet. Rapid Response Systems (primer)
references.scope: Acute change in mental status as a calling criterion; any staff member may call (Screen 4)

stages.label: Act
stages.title: What do you do right now?

calls.410: I need to use the bathroom. Now, please.
calls.412: I feel shaky and jittery. Something's off.
calls.416: My ride got here early. Can I go home?

coverageOptions.text: Dee, 414's pressure is dropping and I'm going now. Can you take 412: get his 0742 recheck, reassess him and act on it under the protocol? And watch 410 and 416 until 0800.
coverageOptions.ack: Got it. 412 at 0742, and I'm watching 410 and 416 until 0800.
coverageOptions.feedback: A nurse who is free has accepted 412 and your other rooms out loud.

coverageOptions.text: Priya, can you take 412's 0742 recheck and reassessment as your short task? Dee, can you watch 410 and 416 until 0800?
coverageOptions.ack: Priya: Yes, that's my one task. I'll call you with the result. Dee: Watching 410 and 416 until 0800. When Priya finishes at 0745, I can take 412 through 0800 if she hands him over to me.
coverageOptions.feedback: Two nurses, each within what they offered. Priya's task ends at 0745; 412 still needs Dee's explicit handback.

coverageOptions.text: Jordan, get 412's glucose at 0742 and give the number straight to Dee. Dee, can you see him with that number, act under the protocol, and watch 410 and 416?
coverageOptions.ack: Jordan: 0742, number to Dee. Dee: Got it. I'll go see him with Jordan's number, and watch 410 and 416 until 0800.
coverageOptions.feedback: Jordan collects the number. A named nurse who has accepted the job reassesses him and decides what's next.

coverageOptions.text: Jordan, get 412's glucose at 0742 and call me with the number.
coverageOptions.feedback: Jordan can collect the number, but he's still shaky and you'll be busy with 414. Name a nurse who can see him and act on it, and ask someone to watch your other rooms.

coverageOptions.text: Finish what you are doing first, then go to 414.
coverageOptions.feedback: A rising heart rate and falling pressure after surgery shouldn't wait. Hand off what you're doing and go.

coverageOptions.text: Jordan, can you check 414's dressing and tell me if it looks bad?
coverageOptions.feedback: Assessing what the dressing and the patient's change mean is a nursing responsibility. A qualified nurse must respond to 414's deterioration without waiting for Jordan's judgment.

410.priya: I'll help her to the bathroom.

412.priya: On my way to 412. I'll call you with what I find; I have to hand him back at 0730.

416.priya: I'll start her teaching if her papers are ready and tell you where I got to.

410.you: You can help her. Jordan could also assist with clear directions and follow-up.
410.priya: Priya can take this call, though Jordan could assist with clear directions and follow-up.
410.jordanA: Jordan has specific fall-safety directions and knows what change to report.
410.jordanB: Name her fall risk, how to assist her and what to report back.
410.hold: The message discourages getting up alone, but a high-fall-risk patient still waits for help.

412.you: A nurse responds to the new symptoms now.
412.priya: Priya offered one call, accepted 412 and will hand him back at 0730.
412.jordan: Jordan may collect a glucose value under this unit's policy, but cannot independently assess or decide what to do for a symptomatic patient. No nurse was sent to 412.
412.hold: A symptomatic patient is waiting without a nurse. Send a qualified nurse now.

416.you: A nurse can start her discharge teaching.
416.priya: Priya can start teaching within her offered window if the papers are ready and tell you where she stopped.
416.jordan: Jordan can reinforce completed teaching, not provide discharge teaching.
416.holdA: She has a specific update and a realistic next check-in.
416.holdB: A vague promise leaves her unsure when a nurse will return.

helpOptions.label: Call rapid response
helpOptions.note: Any staff member with significant concern can call

helpOptions.label: Reinforce the dressing and recheck vitals in 15 minutes first

hold416.A: Your nurse knows your ride is here. They'll be in for your discharge teaching by about 0750.
hold416.B: Your nurse will be there soon.

jordanDirections.A: She's a high fall risk. Use her walker, stay with her the whole time, leave her with the call light in reach and the bed low, and tell me right away if she's dizzy or in more pain.
jordanDirections.B: Can you help 410 to the bathroom?

looseEnds.title: 412 / Mr. Okafor
looseEnds.accepted: Check in on him when you can, and make sure the treating team knows about this morning's low so they can review his plan under your protocol.
looseEnds.acceptedFeedback: This follow-up keeps the morning low on the treating team’s radar; it stays queued until coverage is confirmed.
looseEnds.other: He's back up. Nothing more needed.
looseEnds.otherFeedback: A normal recheck isn't the end. The team should know about the low so they can decide whether his plan needs to change.

looseEnds.title: 414 / Your role
looseEnds.accepted: Stay with his care: carry out new orders as they come, keep reassessing and report how he responds.
looseEnds.acceptedFeedback: The team is here, and you remain responsible for reassessment and reporting.
looseEnds.other: The team has it now. Head back to your other rooms.
looseEnds.otherFeedback: He's still your patient. Reassessing and reporting stay with you.

looseEnds.title: Coverage / 410, 412, 416
looseEnds.accepted: Dee, can you continue covering 410, 412 and 416 through 0830 while I stay with 414? Please call if anything changes. I'll let Priya know.
looseEnds.acceptedFeedback: The request names the rooms and end time. Coverage is not confirmed until Dee accepts out loud.
looseEnds.otherFeedback: Coverage ends at 0800. Stable patients still need a nurse watching. Get a named nurse's acceptance before treating the loop as closed.

looseEnds.title: 416 / Ms. Whitfield
looseEnds.accepted: Ask the confirmed covering nurse to update her with a realistic time, and finish her teaching as soon as a nurse is free.
looseEnds.acceptedFeedback: This follow-up asks for an updated expectation and nurse-led teaching; it stays queued until coverage is confirmed.
looseEnds.other: Ask Jordan to go over her discharge papers so she can leave.
looseEnds.otherFeedback: Teaching needs a nurse. Jordan can reinforce teaching but can't provide it.

looseEnds.title: Jordan / delegated work
looseEnds.accepted: Thank Jordan for flagging 414 fast. Tell her you'll take 414's vitals yourself while he's changing, and to tell you right away about any change in your other patients.

  id: 'drowsy-patient-r2',
  title: 'The Drowsy Patient',
  reviewStatus: 'Independent nurse approval reported by the founder',
  report: 'Good morning. Report just ended. You have 3 patients on a med-surg unit.',
  patients: [
    { id: '12', age: '71-year-old', label: 'COPD / pneumonia', report: '71-year-old with COPD, admitted 2 days ago for pneumonia. On oxygen by nasal cannula; the flow was turned up overnight because "his sats were dipping." "He\'s been really sleepy since about 0400, but his sats are great, 97%. Probably just tired, he didn\'t sleep well."', result: 'Correct', feedback: 'A new change in level of consciousness is never "just tired" until you prove it. "Great sats" in a patient with COPD whose oxygen was just turned up is a cue, not reassurance.' },
    { id: '14', age: '45-year-old', label: 'Post-op day 1', report: '45-year-old, post-op day 1 after laparoscopic abdominal surgery. Pain 7/10, asking for pain medication. Vitals stable at 0600.', result: 'Not first', feedback: "Pain matters. Let Room 14 know you'll be back soon, or ask a colleague to check in. But pain with stable vitals is expected post-op; new drowsiness is not." },
    { id: '9', age: '58-year-old', label: 'Discharge teaching', report: '58-year-old admitted for cellulitis, going home this morning. Needs discharge teaching. Stable overnight.', result: 'Not first', feedback: 'Stable and expected. Discharge teaching can wait until your sicker patients are safe.' },
  ],
  charts: { id: 'charts', text: 'Review all three charts at the station first', result: 'Not first', feedback: 'Report already flagged a change in consciousness. See the patient.' },
  bedside: "You're at Room 12's bedside. Tap each finding to see it.",
  cuePrompt: 'Which findings worry you most right now? Select all that apply.',
  cues: [
    { id: 'consciousness', label: 'Consciousness', text: 'Opens his eyes to his name, then drifts off mid-sentence', tier: 'essential' },
    { id: 'headache', label: 'What he tells you', text: 'Says he has a headache', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'breathing', label: 'Breathing', text: 'Respiratory rate 10, shallow', tier: 'essential' },
    { id: 'saturation', label: 'Oxygen saturation', text: 'SpO2 97% on nasal cannula', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'heart', label: 'Heart rate', text: 'Heart rate 108, sinus tachycardia on the monitor', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'pressure', label: 'Blood pressure', text: 'BP 152/90', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'temperature', label: 'Temperature', text: 'Temp 38.2°C (100.8°F)', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'skin', label: 'Skin', text: 'Skin warm and flushed', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'sounds', label: 'Breath sounds', text: 'Coarse crackles, right lower lobe', tier: 'supporting' },
    { id: 'glucose', label: 'Point-of-care glucose', text: 'Point-of-care glucose 132', tier: 'neutral' },
    { id: 'mar', label: 'Medication record', text: 'MAR: an as-needed sedating cough medication was given at 0300', tier: 'supporting' },
  ],
  essentialFeedback: 'Declining consciousness plus inadequate breathing is the problem that matters most.',
  supportingFeedback: 'They support the picture of inadequate ventilation, and sedation, infection and fever can all make breathing worse.',
  glucoseFeedback: "A gentle note: it doesn't explain the drowsiness.",
  teaching: 'SpO2 estimates arterial oxygen saturation. It does not measure how effectively a patient eliminates CO2. CO2 retention is a strong concern here, but not yet a confirmed cause.',
  actions: [
    { id: 'escalate', text: "Stay with him. Check his airway and breathing: rouse him, sit him upright, count his respirations, watch his effort. Call for help: activate rapid response per your facility's criteria and notify the provider.", result: 'Correct', feedback: "A new change in mental status with slow, shallow breathing meets typical rapid response criteria. Any staff member can call; you don't need permission. Act on the patient; labs come second." },
    { id: 'wait', text: 'Wait for the ABG drawn at 0645 to result, then decide', result: 'No', feedback: 'The patient in front of you is the emergency. A pending lab should never delay escalation.' },
    { id: 'increase', text: "Turn the oxygen up because he's drowsy", result: 'No', feedback: 'More oxygen can worsen CO2 retention in this patient. Oxygen changes follow orders or protocol.' },
    { id: 'stop', text: "Turn the oxygen off because it's causing the problem", result: 'No, unsafe', feedback: 'Stopping oxygen suddenly can drop oxygen levels dangerously. Changes follow orders or protocol.' },
    { id: 'sleep', text: 'Let him sleep and recheck in an hour, his oxygen is fine', result: 'No', feedback: 'This is the trap the scenario teaches. His oxygen is fine; his breathing is not.' },
    { id: 'other', text: 'Medicate Room 14 first, then come back', result: 'No', feedback: 'Room 14 is stable. Room 12 is getting worse now.' },
  ],
  abgArrival: 'The rapid response team arrives within minutes and starts evaluating him. While they work, the ABG drawn at 0645 under an existing order results.',
  abg: [
    { label: 'pH', value: '7.26', unit: '', range: '7.35 to 7.45' },
    { label: 'PaCO2', value: '68', unit: 'mmHg', range: '35 to 45' },
    { label: 'HCO3', value: '30', unit: 'mEq/L', range: '22 to 26' },
    { label: 'PaO2', value: '88', unit: 'mmHg (on oxygen)', range: '80 to 100' },
  ],
  interpretations: [
    { id: 'partial', text: 'Respiratory acidosis with an elevated bicarbonate', result: 'Correct', feedback: 'pH 7.26 shows acidemia; PaCO2 68 identifies a respiratory acidifying process. HCO3 30 is elevated. Compensation can raise bicarbonate, but this result alone does not establish chronic CO2 retention or exclude a mixed disorder.' },
    { id: 'uncompensated', text: 'Respiratory acidosis, uncompensated', result: 'Close', feedback: 'The respiratory process is right, but HCO3 is elevated, not unchanged. Acute buffering can already raise bicarbonate; its value alone does not tell us the duration or adequacy of compensation.' },
    { id: 'full', text: 'Respiratory acidosis, fully compensated', result: 'No', feedback: 'The pH is still acidemic at 7.26. Compensation moves pH toward normal; it does not necessarily restore a normal pH. A normal-range pH would not, by itself, establish appropriate compensation or exclude a mixed disorder.' },
    { id: 'metabolic', text: 'Metabolic alkalosis', result: 'No', feedback: 'A pH below 7.35 is acidemia, not the name of the underlying process. The high PaCO2 supports respiratory acidosis. Elevated HCO3 does not make metabolic alkalosis the primary explanation; a concurrent metabolic process still needs context.' },
    { id: 'normal', text: 'Normal ABG, PaO2 is fine', result: 'No', feedback: 'PaO2 88 on supplemental oxygen does not make this ABG normal. Acidemia and elevated PaCO2 remain important, and PaO2 does not measure ventilation.' },
  ],
  deeper: 'In a simple respiratory acidosis, HCO3 typically rises about 1 to 2 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2 acutely, and about 3 to 4 with chronic renal compensation, relative to a usual baseline near PaCO2 40 and HCO3 24. These are approximate checks, not diagnoses. HCO3 30 does not prove chronic retention or acute-on-chronic disease. Prior blood gases, chemistry, timing and other clinical findings are needed; a mixed disorder remains possible.',
  sbarPrompt: 'The provider calls back while the team is at the bedside. Which SBAR is strongest?',
  sbars: [
    { id: 'a', parts: [
      ['S', "I'm the nurse for Room 12, a 71-year-old with COPD and pneumonia. He's become hard to keep awake since about 0400, and I've activated a rapid response."],
      ['B', 'His oxygen was turned up overnight, and he got an as-needed sedating cough medication at 0300.'],
      ['A', "RR 10 and shallow, SpO2 97% on oxygen, HR 108, BP 152/90, temp 38.2. New headache, flushed skin. ABG at 0645: pH 7.26, PaCO2 68, HCO3 30, PaO2 88. I'm concerned his ventilation is inadequate."],

    { id: 'c', text: 'A full list of every vital sign and lab since admission, with no stated concern or request.', result: 'All data, no message', feedback: "The provider has to guess what you're worried about." },

  outcome: [

    ['0750', "You reassess Room 14's pain."],
    ['0815', "You finish Room 9's discharge teaching."],
  ],
  takeaways: [
    'SpO2 estimates arterial oxygen saturation. It does not measure how effectively a patient eliminates CO2. When a patient gets sleepy, check their breathing, not just their sats.',
    "When breathing and consciousness change, act on the patient. Labs confirm; they don't decide whether you call for help.",
  ],
  why: [
    'In some patients with COPD, too much supplemental oxygen can raise CO2. The main reasons: oxygen relaxes blood vessels in poorly ventilated parts of the lung, which worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and oxygen-rich blood holds less CO2 (the Haldane effect). The old "hypoxic drive" explanation plays only a small role.',
    'Other things can slow breathing too: sedating medications, tired breathing muscles, and worsening pneumonia. In a real patient, several may be happening at once.',
    "That's why many providers order a target SpO2 of 88 to 92% for patients at risk of CO2 retention, then adjust it based on blood gases and the individual patient.",

    { id: 'copd', title: 'Abdo WF, Heunks LMA. Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD: myths and facts. Critical Care 16, 323 (2012)', scope: 'V/Q mismatch as the main mechanism, Haldane effect as secondary, hypoxic drive as minor (debrief)' },
